bel-meydenbauer.name: Meydenbauer Bay Park
bel-meydenbauer.blurb: Bellevue's lakefront: a sandy beach and a floating 420-ft crescent pier on Lake Washington with the Seattle skyline across the water.

spawn.note: Beach promenade at the root of the crescent pier looking out over Lake Washington.

extent.description: Beach, floating crescent pier, kayak rental pavilion, paved/unpaved trails up the ravine toward 100th Ave NE / Downtown Park, playground, restroom building.
extent.edges: Private docks/yacht club east; Lake Washington Blvd NE north.
extent.vertical: Ravine climbs ~25 m from the beach to Main St level.

structures.name: Floating crescent pedestrian pier (2019)
structures.form: Curved floating pier with low railings and seating steps, timber/composite deck on pontoons, gently moving with the lake.

structures.name: Sand and gravel beach + lifeguard stand
structures.form: Swimming beach with lifeguards late June–Labor Day.

structures.name: Restroom/kayak pavilion
structures.form: Modern timber-roofed pavilion with restrooms and kayak/SUP rental.

vegetation: Native plantings (sword fern, Oregon grape, red-osier dogwood), madrone and conifers on the ravine slopes
furniture: 32 benches, 7 picnic tables, toilets, drinking fountain, clock (OSM)

lighting.day: Low sun over the lake in the afternoon; sparkling water
lighting.night: Pier lights; Seattle skyline glittering 9 km west

backdrop: Lake Washington, Mercer Island to the SW, Seattle skyline + Space Needle across the lake (W)
Yachts and private docks of Meydenbauer Bay

crowd.density: Low-medium; summer swimmers, paddleboarders, families, sunset strollers.

plaques.title: Ferry landing
plaques.text: From the 1890s until 1921 this was the landing for passenger ferries between Seattle and Bellevue.

plaques.title: First park
plaques.text: In 1953 it became Bellevue's first park; it reopened in March 2019 with an expanded beach and a 420-ft floating crescent pier.

plaques.title: Wildwood Park
plaques.text: The site once hosted Wildwood Park, a dance hall popular with Seattle residents.

interaction.primary: Rent a kayak (short paddle loop inside the bay) or skip stones from the beach.
secondary: Sunset photo of Seattle's skyline across the lake

iconic.frame: Crescent pier curving out with the Seattle skyline on the horizon at sunset

dialogueGeneral.usage: Pedestrian set for the Seattle and Bellevue driving districts and as filler in every spot. ctx: greeting|bumped|photographed|idle|spot|rain|honked_at|near_miss; non-English lines carry orig+lang with English text.

tone.note: "Seattle Freeze": locals are described as "very polite but not particularly friendly" to strangers — keep local NPC lines courteous, brief, low-key; few unprompted chats.
Washington ranked 48th of 50 states for extraversion (2008 study cited by Wikipedia) — locals default to nods, "sorry", "you're good".

Honking is rare and seen as rude: ~3 in 4 Northwest drivers said they rarely or never honk (PEMCO 2017); attitudes softened by 2021 (65% say honking at least somewhat appropriate). NPC reaction to player honking near spots: surprised/disapproving, not aggressive.
Coffee culture: Seattle drinks more coffee than any other US city; espresso small talk is a safe icebreaker.
Rain talk is universal small talk; locals rarely use umbrellas (hoods/rain shells) — common local self-image, unsourced folklore: keep light.

Visitors: Canada was 73% of Seattle's 2.4 M international visitors in 2024; then China, India, UK, South Korea, Germany, Japan, Australia, France, Taiwan — languages used: English, French (Québec), Mandarin, Hindi, Korean, German, Japanese, Spanish (domestic + Latin America).
Indigenous art (totems, Salish Welcome): staff/guides speak respectfully; no jokes about sacred objects.
Guardrails: no stereotypes, accents written phonetically, slurs, politics or alcohol jokes about any group; tourists are curious and happy, locals helpful-but-reserved.
